The order:
The application by the Applicant is struck from the roll for lack of urgency and lack of service on the Respondents.  

Costs are awarded in favour of the second Respondent such cost to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, and;

 The urgent application is removed from the roll and considered finalised.
Reasons for order:

Ambunda J:

The Applicant approached this Court on an urgent basis seeking the orders as set out in the Notice of Motion filed of record and which appears on the e-justice system.  The Applicant is seeking interim relief with a return date and affording an opportunity to the Respondents to show cause why certain orders should not be made final on the return date.  The Applicants approaches this court on a truncated time periods as set out in the Notice of Motion, which indicates that should the Respondents wish to oppose the application, they must do so by 15 December 2025, that answering affidavits to be filed by 17 December and replying Affidavits to be filed by the 19th of December 2025, and that the return date should be the 22nd December 2025.  This is the same date as indicated in the Notice of Motion to be the return date for the rule nisi order sought.  

The second Respondent, cited in the papers, however opposed the matter just before it could be heard.  I must indicate that the matter was set down in terms of the Notice of Motion at 9 o’clock.  However, it could only be heard at 14h15 due to other urgent applications that were lined up as part of the Court’s business.  Therefore, by the time the matter was heard, there was opposition on the papers by the second Respondent.  

The 1st – 4th Applicants were represented by Mr Velikoshi and the second Respondent was represented by Adv Quickfall.  As preliminary factors, I have indicated to Counsel that only two issues needed to be addressed at this point. Firstly, in light of the fact that there is opposition by at least the second Respondent and secondly the issue on service.  I will start with the issue of service and summarise the facts at hand, as well as the arguments by the parties with respect to the issue of service.

Mr Velikoshi conceded that there are no returns of services filed of record and this is in respect of the first Respondent, being the master of the High Court, the second Respondent Mr Schickerling, the third Respondent, the Deputy Sheriff of Windhoek, the fourth Respondent, Mr Anguboyo and the fifth Respondent, being the Registrar of BIPA.  No returns of services has been filed off record as conceded to by Mr Velikoshi and addressed to the Court. Counsel also indicated that the documents have been dispatched to the deputy sheriff for service, but however no returns of services has been obtained. Counsel was in fact unsure whether service has been effected or not.  I say unsure because of the submission that Mr Velikoshi put on record, technically questioning how the second Respondent found himself before Court.  The court indicated to Counsel that, the fact that the second Respondent is in Court should be a blessing despite service not being done on him.  However, I need to put it on record that, that does not take away a party’s obligation to ensure that all parties are served before any Court order may be given and in fact, before a matter may be heard on anything.  The Court however, because of the presence of the second Respondent who, despite not being served, is before court, asked the parties to address the Court only on these two issues: service and urgency. 

Mr Velikoshi argued that the Court may dispense with the requirement for service, despite the parties not being served, despite the parties not being before Court, because in any event the order is only sought against the first and the second Respondent being the Master of the High Court and Mr Schickerling. Mr Velikoshi further made submission to the effect that despite the service, the urgency of the matter should guide the Court into still hearing the parties at least on the issue of urgency and that no prejudice will be done to the Respondents because of the nature of the order sought, being a form of a rule nisi with a return date, still gives the party an opportunity to come and place their cases before Court despite being served.

 Advocate Quickfall on the other end did not agree with this approach despite the fact that his client is in Court. It must be considered that the papers were not served on his client and that initially, he literally got instructions close to an hour before Court, indicating that the truncated time periods were not even enough to put together answering papers for purposes of the hearing.  In any event, Counsel further argued that service, despite this application not being brought as an Ex parte or where the requirement of service was not dispensed with, it is not one such application and the Court cannot waive the requirement for parties to be served.  

It is common cause from the papers that this is not an Ex Parte application and there are no circumstances that would render it necessary for a matter to be heard without service. The Applicant on its own papers does not even seek an order from the Court to condone a non-compliance with the rules of court, especially with regard to service. The next point that was then canvased by the parties and questioned by the Court is the non-appearance of the ordinary prayer in urgent applications to have the manner of service, the time periods within which to serve and notify other parties for purposes of proceedings to be truncated and to be condoned. That prayer is missing from the Applicant’s papers and as Adv Quickfall sets out, there is no basis on which this Court is even asked to condone non-service.  When the Court questioned Mr Velikoshi with regard to the absence of the prayer, Counsel was of the view that the Court may waive that requirement, alternatively incorporated in the further and/or alternative relief that is always sought at the end of every pleading filed with Court.  

The rules of Court and service are quite clear and as Rule 8 indicates how service should be done on persons, whether natural, artificial or corporate or company. The rules of Court are also very clear as to what instances service may be dispensed with especially when an application is brought as an Ex parte where circumstances would render it viable to not serve parties before an order is given.  

 If at all there is one important element of the justice system is to make sure that all parties are brought before Court. A party is brought before Court by firstly notification and that notification has to be done through service in terms of the rules. If service is not done on a party, technically speaking, no order should be given and in fact this Court was not even obliged to hear the parties on anything until there are returns of services filed and that all parties are fully aware of the Court process and procedures, and the matter has been properly set down and for the parties to exercise their rights on whether to oppose or not.  The fact that a rule nisi is being sought with a return date, for the respondents to anticipate the return date which still gives an opportunity to the parties to bring their cases before Court, does not remedy that non-compliance.  It does not take away the obligation of the parties to be served.  

There are exceptional circumstances under which service must be done and in this case the Applicants have not demonstrated any exceptional circumstances why this Court should waive service in these circumstances and for such an order to be granted in their favour. I also do not see any circumstances to justify an order to be made without service being done in all 4 Respondents.  That is beside the fact that the second Respondent is in Court.  

I have indicated at the beginning that ordinarily, this Court would not have heard the parties without proof of service.  Mr Velikoshi however indicated that despite non-service, the urgency of the matter justifies for the Court to hear the case and that service may be waived.  I will then move to the part of whether the Applicant has set out any urgent circumstances which justify for this Court to hear the matter.  I have consistently indicated to Counsel that when a party seeks interim relief on an urgent basis, you are faced with a double requirement to firstly, ensure that the rules pertaining to urgent applications are complied with, thereafter to ensure that the requirements of an interim interdict are then also complied with.  

Rule 73(4) of the rules of Court sets out exactly what a party needs to do in an urgent application.  Rule 73(4) is probably one of the most used rules in Court, so it is not alien to any of the parties.  The parties know exactly what the requirements for Rule 73 are. It indicates that in an affidavit in support of an urgent application, the party must explicitly and not mere lip service to the rule, set out the circumstances which he or she avers renders the matter urgent and the reason why he or she claims he or she could not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. This is the threshold that the Applicant should meet to convince the Court to hear the matter on an urgent basis.  

I have asked Mr Velikoshi to point me to the Founding Affidavit setting out the facts which renders this matter urgent.  I was referred to paragraphs 50 to 57 of the Founding Affidavit. From a careful reading of these paragraphs, they speak to the requirements of an interim interdict.  Counsel, however used the same factual basis to set out the circumstances which in his opinion renders the matter urgent.  I will briefly go through some of the factors that Counsel referred to as rendering this matter urgent.

Firstly, and the bigger portion of his argument speaks to the conduct of the second Respondent in his capacity as either nominee officio or the appointed capacity as liquidator and the type of conduct complained of. I will demonstrate how.  The Applicants in paragraph 50 says, and this speaks to prima facie right in respect of the interim interdict relief, that the second Respondent acted without proper authority, has abused such authority, and has exceeded the scope of any authority he believed to possess or has otherwise improperly obtained such authority.  Accordingly, the second Respondent has acted with impunity to the detriment not only of the second Applicant but also third parties including the employees and banking institutions.  It is manifest that the second Respondent has demonstrated a disregard of a Court order and unless his conduct is interdicted, there is a real risk that he will continue to act with impunity.

The affidavit further sets out that the actions of the second Respondent, and this is from paragraph 51, in his capacity as both receiver and provisional liquidator are unlawful and constitutes a direct infringement of the Applicant’s rights as well as those of third parties.  Furthermore, the second Respondent continues to act irresponsibly and in a manner that is not only bullish but also falls significantly short of the standard of conduct expected of a receiver and or liquidator occupying a position of judicially responsibility. Counsel also during his argument further pointed out that the conduct of the second Respondent specifically in removing assets and restricting the Applicant’s access to bank accounts has the effect of forcing the second Applicant into default of its financial obligations and causes it to seize its business operations.  These conducts are likely to result in the closure of business, loss of employment opportunities for its staff and the imposition of substantial penalties for breach of contractual commitments to its clients.  It was also mentioned of the fact that there is a Notice to Appeal to the Supreme Court which will be rendered futile if the conduct of the second Respondent is allowed to proceed.  

The court persistently asked Mr Velikoshi how the conduct of the first respondent constitute a ground for urgency and that question was asked in light of what the position in law is when it comes to alleged unlawful or ultra vires conduct of a person being used as a basis to approach the Court in an urgent basis. 

 I refer to the matter of Rosmund v Van Hil,l as well as the matter of Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd where the Court has indicated that the averments that the Respondents has acted illegally or will act illegally on their own does not constitute a ground of urgency.  Exceptional circumstances must be shown to exist before urgent relief is granted.  And the Court in the Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd matter said:

    ‘I am of the view that the fact that a litigant or Respondent in particular has embarked on an illegal crusade does not of its own render a matter urgent.  There must be something more than just illegality that warrants the invocation of urgency regime.  As it is, each matter must be pointed out, will turn on its own facts.  The view of the Court was that illegality of an action does not without more render the matter urgent.  There will be circumstances where an illegal action coupled with other considerations may render the matter urgent and there may be other circumstances where the same results does not eventuate to however equate illegality to urgency it is in my conceded view not a correct approach.’

Now, coming back to the facts of this case and having considered the type of conduct that is being complained of by the Applicants, in a nutshell, it can be summarised that the second respondent is seen to be on a frolic of his own and is acting in an unlawful or unwarranted manner.  From the authorities as indicated above, that alone does not constitute urgency.  Did the Applicants prove more circumstances than that?  I think not.  I say so for the following reasons: much has been stated that if this Court order is not granted today for example the Applicant’s business will come to a standstill, people need to be paid, and the second applicant will be defaulting and its payments in respect of the properties and that of his business need to continue. I fail to understand this line of argument because it does not indicate how the conduct of the second respondent contributes to these consequences or how a lack of an urgent order will halt the Applicants’ business, especially in the face of two Court orders of a provisional and final liquidation relating to the Applicants, which already halts the business of the Applicant.  In light of those two orders, it is already ‘not business as usual’.  So, the conduct of the second Respondent can never be imputed to the extent that it is being used as a ground for urgency to indicate that if the matter is not heard on an urgent basis, the Applicant’s business is crumbling.  

The second leg of Rule 73(4) requires of a party to indicate why substantial redress cannot be obtianed at a hearing in due course. From the exchange of the Court with Mr Velikoshi, it became clear that the approach or the focus is more that if the second Respondent is allowed to continue, there will not be much left to savage, that it would be difficult to get back the properties that may be purchased by bona fide purchasers. 

The requirement of Rule 73(4) must be properly understood.  It would mean that if this Court does not give the order today, that will be the end of it, and there is no other remedy that will be available to the Applicant in due course.  It is in that light that the Court needs a party to define and set out a reason why it indicates that it will not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. Clearly, in this matter and it is something that Adv Quickfall also touched on, there are mechanisms and remedies available, for example, to approach the Master of the High Court, to ask for the removal of a liquidator if the parties are of the opinion that a nominee or liquidator or receiver is not acting in accordance with their powers as given  in terms of the appointments by the Master.  So, there are remedies available to the Applicant, this is not the end of the matter.  

The Applicants have not made out a case where this Court should waive the requirement of service.  Secondly, the Applicants have not made out a case as to why this matter should be heard on an urgent basis.  These are all procedural aspects that have not been complied with, and the appropriate order would be to strike the matter from the roll for lack of urgency and service.  

With regard to costs, Mr Quickfall submitted that costs should be given on a punitive scale because the matter should not even be here.  I however refrain from giving a punitive scale because I do not have circumstances warranting any intentional or vexatious conduct on the part of the Applicant, save to have presented a case with procedural pitfalls.  So, costs will follow on a normal scale, such costs to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, in favour of second Respondent, who has at least thus far opposed the matter.  

The order of the Court is then as follows:

The application by the Applicant is struck from the roll for lack of urgency and lack of service on the respondents.  

Costs are awarded in favour of the second Respondent, such cost to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, and;

 The urgent application is removed from the roll and considered finalised.

Mr Velikoshi further made submission to the effect that despite the service, the urgency of the matter should guide the Court into still hearing the parties at least on the issue of urgency and that no prejudice will be done to the Respondents because of the nature of the order sought, being a form of a rule nisi with a return date, still gives the party an opportunity to come and place their cases before Court despite being served.

 Advocate Quickfall on the other end did not agree with this approach despite the fact that his client is in Court. It must be considered that the papers were not served on his client and that initially, he literally got instructions close to an hour before Court, indicating that the truncated time periods were not even enough to put together answering papers for purposes of the hearing.  In any event, Counsel further argued that service, despite this application not being brought as an Ex parte or where the requirement of service was not dispensed with, it is not one such application and the Court cannot waive the requirement for parties to be served.  

It is common cause from the papers that this is not an Ex Parte application and there are no circumstances that would render it necessary for a matter to be heard without service. The Applicant on its own papers does not even seek an order from the Court to condone a non-compliance with the rules of court, especially with regard to service. The next point that was then canvased by the parties and questioned by the Court is the non-appearance of the ordinary prayer in urgent applications to have the manner of service, the time periods within which to serve and notify other parties for purposes of proceedings to be truncated and to be condoned. That prayer is missing from the Applicant’s papers and as Adv Quickfall sets out, there is no basis on which this Court is even asked to condone non-service.  When the Court questioned Mr Velikoshi with regard to the absence of the prayer, Counsel was of the view that the Court may waive that requirement, alternatively incorporated in the further and/or alternative relief that is always sought at the end of every pleading filed with Court.  

The rules of Court and service are quite clear and as Rule 8 indicates how service should be done on persons, whether natural, artificial or corporate or company. The rules of Court are also very clear as to what instances service may be dispensed with especially when an application is brought as an Ex parte where circumstances would render it viable to not serve parties before an order is given.  

 If at all there is one important element of the justice system is to make sure that all parties are brought before Court. A party is brought before Court by firstly notification and that notification has to be done through service in terms of the rules. If service is not done on a party, technically speaking, no order should be given and in fact this Court was not even obliged to hear the parties on anything until there are returns of services filed and that all parties are fully aware of the Court process and procedures, and the matter has been properly set down and for the parties to exercise their rights on whether to oppose or not.  The fact that a rule nisi is being sought with a return date, for the respondents to anticipate the return date which still gives an opportunity to the parties to bring their cases before Court, does not remedy that non-compliance.  It does not take away the obligation of the parties to be served.  

There are exceptional circumstances under which service must be done and in this case the Applicants have not demonstrated any exceptional circumstances why this Court should waive service in these circumstances and for such an order to be granted in their favour. I also do not see any circumstances to justify an order to be made without service being done in all 4 Respondents.  That is beside the fact that the second Respondent is in Court.  

I have indicated at the beginning that ordinarily, this Court would not have heard the parties without proof of service.  Mr Velikoshi however indicated that despite non-service, the urgency of the matter justifies for the Court to hear the case and that service may be waived.  I will then move to the part of whether the Applicant has set out any urgent circumstances which justify for this Court to hear the matter. Rule 73(4) is probably one of the most used rules in Court, so it is not alien to any of the parties.  The parties know exactly what the requirements for Rule 73 are. It indicates that in an affidavit in support of an urgent application, the party must explicitly and not mere lip service to the rule, set out the circumstances which he or she avers renders the matter urgent and the reason why he or she claims he or she could not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. This is the threshold that the Applicant should meet to convince the Court to hear the matter on an urgent basis.  

I have asked Mr Velikoshi to point me to the Founding Affidavit setting out the facts which renders this matter urgent.  I was referred to paragraphs 50 to 57 of the Founding Affidavit. From a careful reading of these paragraphs, they speak to the requirements of an interim interdict.  Counsel, however used the same factual basis to set out the circumstances which in his opinion renders the matter urgent.  I will briefly go through some of the factors that Counsel referred to as rendering this matter urgent.

Firstly, and the bigger portion of his argument speaks to the conduct of the second Respondent in his capacity as either nominee officio or the appointed capacity as liquidator and the type of conduct complained of. I will demonstrate how.  The Applicants in paragraph 50 says, and this speaks to prima facie right in respect of the interim interdict relief, that the second Respondent acted without proper authority, has abused such authority, and has exceeded the scope of any authority he believed to possess or has otherwise improperly obtained such authority.  Accordingly, the second Respondent has acted with impunity to the detriment not only of the second Applicant but also third parties including the employees and banking institutions.  It is manifest that the second Respondent has demonstrated a disregard of a Court order and unless his conduct is interdicted, there is a real risk that he will continue to act with impunity.

The affidavit further sets out that the actions of the second Respondent, and this is from paragraph 51, in his capacity as both receiver and provisional liquidator are unlawful and constitutes a direct infringement of the Applicant’s rights as well as those of third parties.  Furthermore, the second Respondent continues to act irresponsibly and in a manner that is not only bullish but also falls significantly short of the standard of conduct expected of a receiver and or liquidator occupying a position of judicially responsibility. Counsel also during his argument further pointed out that the conduct of the second Respondent specifically in removing assets and restricting the Applicant’s access to bank accounts has the effect of forcing the second Applicant into default of its financial obligations and causes it to seize its business operations.  These conducts are likely to result in the closure of business, loss of employment opportunities for its staff and the imposition of substantial penalties for breach of contractual commitments to its clients.  It was also mentioned of the fact that there is a Notice to Appeal to the Supreme Court which will be rendered futile if the conduct of the second Respondent is allowed to proceed.  

The court persistently asked Mr Velikoshi how the conduct of the first respondent constitute a ground for urgency and that question was asked in light of what the position in law is when it comes to alleged unlawful or ultra vires conduct of a person being used as a basis to approach the Court in an urgent basis. 

 I refer to the matter of Rosmund v Van Hil,l as well as the matter of Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd where the Court has indicated that the averments that the Respondents has acted illegally or will act illegally on their own does not constitute a ground of urgency.  Exceptional circumstances must be shown to exist before urgent relief is granted.  And the Court in the Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd matter said:

    ‘I am of the view that the fact that a litigant or Respondent in particular has embarked on an illegal crusade does not of its own render a matter urgent.  There must be something more than just illegality that warrants the invocation of urgency regime.  As it is, each matter must be pointed out, will turn on its own facts.  The view of the Court was that illegality of an action does not without more render the matter urgent.  There will be circumstances where an illegal action coupled with other considerations may render the matter urgent and there may be other circumstances where the same results does not eventuate to however equate illegality to urgency it is in my conceded view not a correct approach.’

Now, coming back to the facts of this case and having considered the type of conduct that is being complained of by the Applicants, in a nutshell, it can be summarised that the second respondent is seen to be on a frolic of his own and is acting in an unlawful or unwarranted manner.  From the authorities as indicated above, that alone does not constitute urgency.  Did the Applicants prove more circumstances than that?  I think not.  I say so for the following reasons: much has been stated that if this Court order is not granted today for example the Applicant’s business will come to a standstill, people need to be paid, and the second applicant will be defaulting and its payments in respect of the properties and that of his business need to continue. I fail to understand this line of argument because it does not indicate how the conduct of the second respondent contributes to these consequences or how a lack of an urgent order will halt the Applicants’ business, especially in the face of two Court orders of a provisional and final liquidation relating to the Applicants, which already halts the business of the Applicant.  In light of those two orders, it is already ‘not business as usual’.  So, the conduct of the second Respondent can never be imputed to the extent that it is being used as a ground for urgency to indicate that if the matter is not heard on an urgent basis, the Applicant’s business is crumbling.  

The second leg of Rule 73(4) requires of a party to indicate why substantial redress cannot be obtianed at a hearing in due course. From the exchange of the Court with Mr Velikoshi, it became clear that the approach or the focus is more that if the second Respondent is allowed to continue, there will not be much left to savage, that it would be difficult to get back the properties that may be purchased by bona fide purchasers. 

The requirement of Rule 73(4) must be properly understood.  It would mean that if this Court does not give the order today, that will be the end of it, and there is no other remedy that will be available to the Applicant in due course.  It is in that light that the Court needs a party to define and set out a reason why it indicates that it will not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. Clearly, in this matter and it is something that Adv Quickfall also touched on, there are mechanisms and remedies available, for example, to approach the Master of the High Court, to ask for the removal of a liquidator if the parties are of the opinion that a nominee or liquidator or receiver is not acting in accordance with their powers as given  in terms of the appointments by the Master.  So, there are remedies available to the Applicant, this is not the end of the matter.  

The Applicants have not made out a case where this Court should waive the requirement of service.  Secondly, the Applicants have not made out a case as to why this matter should be heard on an urgent basis.  These are all procedural aspects that have not been complied with, and the appropriate order would be to strike the matter from the roll for lack of urgency and service.  

With regard to costs, Mr Quickfall submitted that costs should be given on a punitive scale because the matter should not even be here.  I however refrain from giving a punitive scale because I do not have circumstances warranting any intentional or vexatious conduct on the part of the Applicant, save to have presented a case with procedural pitfalls.  So, costs will follow on a normal scale, such costs to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, in favour of second Respondent, who has at least thus far opposed the matter.  

The order of the Court is then as follows:

The application by the Applicant is struck from the roll for lack of urgency and lack of service on the respondents.  

Costs are awarded in favour of the second Respondent, such cost to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, and;

 The urgent application is removed from the roll and considered finalised.

I also do not see any circumstances to justify an order to be made without service being done in all 4 Respondents.  That is beside the fact that the second Respondent is in Court.  

I have indicated at the beginning that ordinarily, this Court would not have heard the parties without proof of service.  Mr Velikoshi however indicated that despite non-service, the urgency of the matter justifies for the Court to hear the case and that service may be waived.  I will then move to the part of whether the Applicant has set out any urgent circumstances which justify for this Court to hear the matter.  I have consistently indicated to Counsel that when a party seeks interim relief on an urgent basis, you are faced with a double requirement to firstly, ensure that the rules pertaining to urgent applications are complied with, thereafter to ensure that the requirements of an interim interdict are then also complied with.  

Rule 73(4) of the rules of Court sets out exactly what a party needs to do in an urgent application.  Rule 73(4) is probably one of the most used rules in Court, so it is not alien to any of the parties.  The parties know exactly what the requirements for Rule 73 are. It indicates that in an affidavit in support of an urgent application, the party must explicitly and not mere lip service to the rule, set out the circumstances which he or she avers renders the matter urgent and the reason why he or she claims he or she could not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. This is the threshold that the Applicant should meet to convince the Court to hear the matter on an urgent basis.  

I have asked Mr Velikoshi to point me to the Founding Affidavit setting out the facts which renders this matter urgent.  I was referred to paragraphs 50 to 57 of the Founding Affidavit. From a careful reading of these paragraphs, they speak to the requirements of an interim interdict.  Counsel, however used the same factual basis to set out the circumstances which in his opinion renders the matter urgent.  I will briefly go through some of the factors that Counsel referred to as rendering this matter urgent.

Firstly, and the bigger portion of his argument speaks to the conduct of the second Respondent in his capacity as either nominee officio or the appointed capacity as liquidator and the type of conduct complained of. I will demonstrate how.  The Applicants in paragraph 50 says, and this speaks to prima facie right in respect of the interim interdict relief, that the second Respondent acted without proper authority, has abused such authority, and has exceeded the scope of any authority he believed to possess or has otherwise improperly obtained such authority.  Accordingly, the second Respondent has acted with impunity to the detriment not only of the second Applicant but also third parties including the employees and banking institutions.  It is manifest that the second Respondent has demonstrated a disregard of a Court order and unless his conduct is interdicted, there is a real risk that he will continue to act with impunity.

The affidavit further sets out that the actions of the second Respondent, and this is from paragraph 51, in his capacity as both receiver and provisional liquidator are unlawful and constitutes a direct infringement of the Applicant’s rights as well as those of third parties.  Furthermore, the second Respondent continues to act irresponsibly and in a manner that is not only bullish but also falls significantly short of the standard of conduct expected of a receiver and or liquidator occupying a position of judicially responsibility. Counsel also during his argument further pointed out that the conduct of the second Respondent specifically in removing assets and restricting the Applicant’s access to bank accounts has the effect of forcing the second Applicant into default of its financial obligations and causes it to seize its business operations.  These conducts are likely to result in the closure of business, loss of employment opportunities for its staff and the imposition of substantial penalties for breach of contractual commitments to its clients.  It was also mentioned of the fact that there is a Notice to Appeal to the Supreme Court which will be rendered futile if the conduct of the second Respondent is allowed to proceed.  

The court persistently asked Mr Velikoshi how the conduct of the first respondent constitute a ground for urgency and that question was asked in light of what the position in law is when it comes to alleged unlawful or ultra vires conduct of a person being used as a basis to approach the Court in an urgent basis. 

 I refer to the matter of Rosmund v Van Hil,l as well as the matter of Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd where the Court has indicated that the averments that the Respondents has acted illegally or will act illegally on their own does not constitute a ground of urgency.  Exceptional circumstances must be shown to exist before urgent relief is granted.  And the Court in the Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd matter said:

    ‘I am of the view that the fact that a litigant or Respondent in particular has embarked on an illegal crusade does not of its own render a matter urgent.  There must be something more than just illegality that warrants the invocation of urgency regime.  As it is, each matter must be pointed out, will turn on its own facts.  The view of the Court was that illegality of an action does not without more render the matter urgent.  There will be circumstances where an illegal action coupled with other considerations may render the matter urgent and there may be other circumstances where the same results does not eventuate to however equate illegality to urgency it is in my conceded view not a correct approach.’

Now, coming back to the facts of this case and having considered the type of conduct that is being complained of by the Applicants, in a nutshell, it can be summarised that the second respondent is seen to be on a frolic of his own and is acting in an unlawful or unwarranted manner.  From the authorities as indicated above, that alone does not constitute urgency.  Did the Applicants prove more circumstances than that?  I think not.  I say so for the following reasons: much has been stated that if this Court order is not granted today for example the Applicant’s business will come to a standstill, people need to be paid, and the second applicant will be defaulting and its payments in respect of the properties and that of his business need to continue. I fail to understand this line of argument because it does not indicate how the conduct of the second respondent contributes to these consequences or how a lack of an urgent order will halt the Applicants’ business, especially in the face of two Court orders of a provisional and final liquidation relating to the Applicants, which already halts the business of the Applicant.  In light of those two orders, it is already ‘not business as usual’.  So, the conduct of the second Respondent can never be imputed to the extent that it is being used as a ground for urgency to indicate that if the matter is not heard on an urgent basis, the Applicant’s business is crumbling.  

The second leg of Rule 73(4) requires of a party to indicate why substantial redress cannot be obtianed at a hearing in due course. From the exchange of the Court with Mr Velikoshi, it became clear that the approach or the focus is more that if the second Respondent is allowed to continue, there will not be much left to savage, that it would be difficult to get back the properties that may be purchased by bona fide purchasers. 

The requirement of Rule 73(4) must be properly understood.  It would mean that if this Court does not give the order today, that will be the end of it, and there is no other remedy that will be available to the Applicant in due course.  It is in that light that the Court needs a party to define and set out a reason why it indicates that it will not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. Clearly, in this matter and it is something that Adv Quickfall also touched on, there are mechanisms and remedies available, for example, to approach the Master of the High Court, to ask for the removal of a liquidator if the parties are of the opinion that a nominee or liquidator or receiver is not acting in accordance with their powers as given  in terms of the appointments by the Master.  So, there are remedies available to the Applicant, this is not the end of the matter.  

The Applicants have not made out a case where this Court should waive the requirement of service.  Secondly, the Applicants have not made out a case as to why this matter should be heard on an urgent basis.  These are all procedural aspects that have not been complied with, and the appropriate order would be to strike the matter from the roll for lack of urgency and service.  

With regard to costs, Mr Quickfall submitted that costs should be given on a punitive scale because the matter should not even be here.  I however refrain from giving a punitive scale because I do not have circumstances warranting any intentional or vexatious conduct on the part of the Applicant, save to have presented a case with procedural pitfalls.  So, costs will follow on a normal scale, such costs to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, in favour of second Respondent, who has at least thus far opposed the matter.  

The order of the Court is then as follows:

The application by the Applicant is struck from the roll for lack of urgency and lack of service on the respondents.  

Costs are awarded in favour of the second Respondent, such cost to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, and;

 The urgent application is removed from the roll and considered finalised.
